Archives – October 30, 2023

The wonders of the Photography and Heritage Media Library, of the Cartier-Bresson Foundation The treasures of the Casagrande collection and the little joys of research Marcel Arthaud/Henri Cartier-Bresson/Roger Parry

When writing Photo Agencies A French History , which I did over several years, I was looking for unpublished documents to illustrate the work. With 650 pages of text, we had to forget about images except for the cover. However, I had several hitherto unseen and interesting documents. Jean-Jaques Naudet suggested that I share some of them with the readers of his site.

My friend Bernard Lebrun gave me some nuggets about the liberation of Paris. I only had the photographs and no information about them. Bernard disappeared too soon, how could we find their author?

The first photograph shows three photographers: Henri Cartier-Bresson, a war correspondent, and Henri Membré with his FFI armband (document no. 1). Membré, independent photographer, active during the Occupation, structured and coordinated as best he could the reportages of around thirty photographers to cover the insurrection in the different districts of Paris. His ambition was to create a new agency, Photo Presse Libération, and thus turn the page on four years of occupation. Accompanied by FFI, he requisitioned photographers from agencies active since June 1940. The shots were then taken by the Photo Presse Libération pool, photographers from Agence France Presse, The War Picture Pool, independent photographers and amateurs. After the Liberation, Membré set up the AFP photographic service and imposed his photographers. He took over as technical director of the service, with Roger Parry as deputy.

Document No. 1, Henri Cartier-Bresson, a war correspondent, Henri Membré, Paris August 1944. © Estate Marcel Arthaud, Nicéphore Niépce museum, City of Chalon-sur-Saône.

I was looking for other photographs that would allow me to identify the first one. Thinking that it could be from Roger Parry, a close friend of Membré, I did a search on the website of the Heritage and Photography media library which keeps the collection donated by his widow Madeleine Parry in 1993. I found three inverted negatives where HCB figured.

The director of the MPP, Gilles Désiré dit Gosset, authorized me to publish the documents free of charge.

The first negative presents the same three, in the same place as on document no. 1, photographing themselves under the amused gaze of onlookers (document no. 2). Roger Parry could therefore be the photographer of document n°1. But photograph no. 1 does not appear in the Parry collection.

Document No. 2, the caption states: “A photographer photographs a soldier himself equipped with a camera. » Henri Cartier-Bresson from behind, a war correspondent, Henri Membré, Paris August 1944, © Donation Roger Parry, Ministry of Culture (France), Media Library of Heritage and Photography, RMN-GP broadcast.

Finally, to identify document no. 1 communicated by Bernard Lebrun, it was his colleague and friend Michel Lefebvre who put me on the trail of the Casagrande Collection. The collector told me that on the back of the photograph appeared the name of the photographer: Marcel Arthaud. A contact sheet on which the Arthaud stamp is affixed confirmed this. I had gone the wrong way with Parry. It was Arthaud, whose collection is kept at the Nicéphore Niépce museum, in Chalon-sur-Saône. The director, Sylvain Besson and the rights holders authorised me to publish the document free of charge.

A second negative by Roger Parry where we recognize Cartier-Bresson from behind, perfectly identifiable, always wearing the same suit and his leather case slung over his shoulder, aroused my curiosity (document no. 3). Looking at them, he passes a group of German officers and soldiers who have just surrendered. One of them, in the back, raises his hands in the air. Did Cartier-Bresson take the photograph? Obviously he doesn’t seem interested. As for Parry, he spotted HCB and this is undoubtedly the reason for him shooting.

Document No. 3, the caption states: “August 26, 1944. Liberation parade: German prisoners and FFI”. Henri Cartier-Bresson passes in front of surrendering Germans, Paris August 1944, © Donation Roger Parry, Ministry of Culture (France), Media Library of Heritage and Photography, RMN-GP broadcast.

I made an appointment with Aude Raimbault in charge of the collections at the Cartier-Bresson Foundation. As always, a great professional, she had prepared the contact sheets for the Liberation of Paris. I looked at them all once, then examined them more carefully one by one. Two sequences caught my attention. On plate no. 0125, six photographs from numbers 22 to 27 show soldiers and officers, arms in the air. They leave a building in small groups, based on contacts. On No. 22, selected by Cartier-Bresson, a soldier clearly stands out from the cohort, but none resembles the Germans on document No. 3. However, the elements of the building, particularly the arrangement of the windows , recall those in Arthaud’s photograph, but this index is insufficient. Men are all different.

It is two contacts n° 20 and 21 on plate n° 0127 that give me the answer that strip is at the end of the plate picture number 19 is taken in a different place than that of number 20. On this last one (document n° 4) selected by the author with a red pencil mark there are soldiers and officers grouped in the same way as in document n° 3 the men are are different except two, the german officer faced on and the FFI with the black tie cigarette in hand. The important element is the inscription on the window pane « European Social Movement» created in 1940 by Pierre Constantini cofounder with Jacques Doriot of the french legion against bolshevism several nazis had to take care of the functionning of the organisation. Aude Raimbault also allowed me to use the document 4 free of charge.

Document No. 4, scan taken from contact sheet No. 127, Libération de Paris. © Henri Cartier-Bresson Foundation / Magnum Photos

Cartier Bresson therefore took the photograph well. He even dedicated eight shots to this sequence. In Arthaud’s photograph, is he arriving or leaving? Has he already operated or not? We do not know. The images must retain a little of their mystery.

On the other hand, on the HCB contact sheets, there is no trace of the photograph in which he shoots at the same time as Membré and the American war correspondent (document no. 2). Was the negative lost or was Cartier-Bresson faking it? Film was rare, was the picture worth it?

Document No. 5, the caption states: “Men and women seated at table, celebrate the victory”.

At the Membré PC, on the left, during a lunch at 100 rue Réaumur where the Committee for the Liberation of Photographic Reporters is based. In the center, probably the press correspondent, Cartier-Bresson in the background. © Donation Roger Parry, Ministry of Culture (France), Heritage and Photography Media Library, RMN-GP broadcast.

From the press correspondent, probably American, (documents no. 1 and no. 2) I still know nothing. On contact sheet no. 125 of Cartier Bresson, there is a contact where there is a correspondent, with the same camera, posing in a room in front of a drawing of Hitler, but is it the same? hard to say. As on Roger Parry’s negative (document no. 5), the character in the center resembles the one photographed by HCB in front of a portrait of Hitler.

If you recognize the correspondent….

We don’t stop research, we suspend it.

Françoise Denoyelle

article_text:
Films and events

Galas

Being Heumann

British actor Ruth Madeley is outstanding as Judith Heumann, the activist who helped fight for anti-discrimination laws for individuals with disabilities, in CODA director Siân Heder’s enthralling film.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Siân Heder

Screenwriters Siân Heder, Rebekah Taussig

With Ruth Madeley, Madeline Delp, Mark Ruffalo, Dylan O’Brien, Rob Delaney

USA 2026. 127min

Courtesy of Apple TV

Language English

Access information

Monday 12 October 17:45

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Tuesday 13 October 14:15

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Friday 16 October 14:50

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Featuring an exceptional ensemble, including Mark Ruffalo and Dylan O’Brien, Heder’s precisely rendered drama recreates the battle between government officials and the activists, culminating in their 28-day takeover of San Francisco’s Federal Building in 1977. What emerges is a vision of a tenacious, witty collective of history-makers whose groundbreaking act of resistance was instrumental in bringing much-needed social change.

Kristy Matheson

Content advice

Contains scenes of ableism and drug use.

Contains ableist attitudes and language.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

The Slightest Touch

The power of friendship and connection is explored in Rachel Fleit’s soulful and life-affirming documentary, featuring Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell.

Rebellion

Revolution is the beat that drums through this electrifying story about the landmark case against the Bradford 12.

Adam Pearson: Zero Intention of Living Quietly

Actor, broadcaster, and leading disability advocate Adam Pearson joins us to discuss his career and his influential advocacy work for more inclusive storytelling and authentic representation.

article_text:
Selma Blair has been charged with second-degree assault after being arrested following a violent incident on a Delta flight on Sunday, according to Queens Criminal Court. The actress posted $20,000 in bail, paid by credit card, and was released on Monday.

The “Cruel Intentions” actress was arrested on Monday by a Port Authority police officer for allegedly attacking an officer and a nurse following her removal from the Delta plane on Sunday. She then appeared in Queens Criminal Court Monday evening before Judge Indira D. Khan, per court documents viewed by Variety. Blair pleaded not guilty to the state charges, but faces separate federal charges for the airplane incident.

On the plane, she allegedly punched one flight attendant and bit another while heading from Los Angeles to New York. Blair also attempted to open the plane door while in the air. Law enforcement was waiting for the 54-year-old “Legally Blonde” actress at John F. Kennedy airport, where police took her into custody and transported her to a hospital for evaluation. Two flight attendants reported injuries, with one receiving treatment at a hospital.

After the incident, a representative for Blair told Variety : “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

In 2016, Blair experienced a previous outburst while on a plane, during which she was removed from a flight on a stretcher while traveling with her then 4-year-old son after she “had a total psychotic blackout,” as she described it. Blair attributed the incident to drinking a glass of wine and taking a pill. “It was horrible and frightening, and I had empathy for myself actually afterward because it was actually so out of character for me, especially because I’m a mother,” she said at the time.

Source: Millie Turner

Mia Bays

Mia Bays is feeling energised as she comes to the end of her five-year tenure as the director of the BFI Filmmaking Fund.

“I’m excited. I’m ready to do something else, to go back to the creative crucible,” she says.

Bays, who previously headed the film charity Birds’ Eye View (now Reclaim The Frame), joined the BFI in 2021 at the tail end of the pandemic on a three-year contract, later extended to five. She steered the fund – investing National Lottery ‘good cause’ money – through choppy post-pandemic waters to see the BFI claim its highest-ever number of Bafta nominations in 2025, for films including Kneecap and Bird .

She helped to expand the view of what a ‘UK’ film looks like, backing India-shot films Santosh , Our Share Of Sand and Sister Midnight, and Nigeria-shot My Father’s Shadow – which won a Bafta – and Lady .

Bays also took a keen interest in diversifying the backgrounds of those who received funding, and the BFI’s stats show improvement under her leadership, particularly for individuals with disabilities.

Recipients of production funding who self-identify as disabled (writer, producer or director) increased from 6% in the 2021-2 funding cycle to 42% in 2025-6. In 2023-4, the fund began reporting class, with 28% of recipients identifying as working class in the initial cycle, up to 36% in 2025-6.

Bays also restructured production funding into the Discovery Fund for debuts below £3.5m, and the Impact Fund for more ambitious projects, over £3.5m. She oversaw the introduction of the Creative Challenge Fund, supporting UK-wide labs to enable decentralised project development, and the Future Takes scheme for high-budget shorts, in partnership with Film4.

The inevitable challenges included a fall in the total annual BFI film funding pot to £20.3m per year, down from £25m, and ongoing debate about whether the films have drifted too far from what audiences will pay to go and see at the cinema.

“The job is relentless,” admits Bays of the intense industry scrutiny of being the face of a publicly supported funding institution. “There is no let-up.”

As she hands over to incoming fund head Isabel Davis, Bays talks to Screen about the choices she made to balance “finite resources with infinite need”, why steering a slate of UK Dogma films is her next move, and takes the opportunity to correct several widespread misunderstandings about the BFI.

What has surprised you most about the BFI role?

You become a symbol of an organisation to such an extent that what you did before is forgotten, or almost erased. You’re a symbol of an organisation that does an enormous amount of work across the whole ecosystem. I’m surprised about how many people thought I ran the London Film Festival too, and the archive, and programmed BFI Southbank.

What are you most proud of?

The work we did to establish trust in the system, so that there is clarity, consistency and care. I hope that people felt that that care was being centred. That we’ve thought about how it feels when people approach us. I still don’t think any institution gets this right. It’s hard. There’s a power imbalance.

I do feel like there is more transparency with which we are trying to operate. I would hope there is a little bit of a shift to seeing us not as gatekeepers, but as stewards. I prefer that term.

You used the word ‘battle’ recently . What have those key battles been, and how have you navigated them?

It’s the emotional and political complexity of public funding and National Lottery funding, which is particularly what I’m responsible for, and how that is viewed, and the particular benefits it carries with it, from the industry impact to the audience impact.

There are a lot of considerations, and it takes a lot of thinking about, and often battling through. You’re balancing finite resources with infinite need. When I said battle, it wasn’t necessarily with people or parties, but the relentless nature of the job.

How do you feel the restructured funds have worked?

I feel proud of that work – having a number of different funds, making it clear that the different funds have different priorities, and decentralising development with the Challenge Fund so you can come to us, but you also have other options. There are other gatekeepers, stewards of the money.

Sectioning the production fund into Discovery and Impact, so it’s clear we have intentions to support debuts and we have intentions to support people at other stages of their career. Clarity was needed. You’re always navigating so much scrutiny and expectation, it’s incredible how much misinformation spreads and sets in.

One point that comes up with producers is the BFI no longer comes first in, as cornerstone financing. Is this correct, or an example of misinformation?

No, that’s not true. Because the industry is so uncertain, people hold onto truths and don’t check. There are lots of different stages we enter films.

The Incomer – we were there at the beginning, we developed that with Screen Scotland, that’s cornerstone finance. We board lots of things with Film4 and BBC Film, they are usually the first cornerstone but us boarding commits to a greenlight.

A phrase you’ve used a few times is the BFI’s National Lottery funding is there to address ‘market failure’. Can you explain what you mean by that phrase, and if you stand by it?

It’s baked into what National Lottery money has to be spent on. It’s not my invention. It’s ‘good cause’ funding.

Obviously, it’s an interpretation of what you mean by what is a ‘good cause’. It has to be there where the commercial sector isn’t, and that doesn’t mean to say that we’re making films that aren’t commercially viable. All films have to have a route to market. Impact Fund applications have to have a sales agent attached, so there has to be some gauge of international appeal.

As it is so hard to get films funded now, there are growing calls that the BFI should be backing more ‘commercial’ and ‘audience-facing’ films.

A film like The Incomer got picked up by Focus/Universal and is getting a significant release. Kneecap had significant success [grossing £2.2m at the UK-Ireland box office]. So we are [backing commercial films]. We’ve got three or four quite significant-to-mid-range budget films coming through that people just haven’t seen yet.

There is a balance. We are triggered by applications. We can’t go out and solicit. We’re not able to do that. We can’t commission. We can’t buy in IP. We’re dependent on the films knocking on our door.

How closely are you working with your successor, Isabel Davis?

We’re doing a handover, and there are certain times where it’s best for me to not be there and for her to take the temperature herself. Other times, I’m in the meetings.

Your next move is to shepherd the first Dogma UK slate. Why were you drawn to that?

What I’ve observed so much is how hard it is for established filmmakers to sustain their creativity, to have a career, to have longevity in it, to not be broken by the experiences.

We’re in the process of building our model. We’ve got our filmmaker lineup.

Is there anything else in the pipeline?

It will be mainly Dogma. I’m interested in doing some consultancy. I’m talking to some other national funds about whether I can help as a recovering film fund head.

I’m interested in executive producing. There is a space that I’m interested in filling; often I’ve seen it on films that we’ve funded, someone who might be an elder can be helpful for the filmmaker navigating experiences that they have not been through before.

And you’re moving out of London…

I am very excited about that. I’m moving to the southwest, I will base my business in Bristol and live in Exeter. That’s a real milestone for me – I’ve been in London my whole life. Relocating, changing my business base, is a deliberate choice to live the decentralisation we are talking about so much. That’s the political climate – if we want regional film cultures to thrive, some of us might need to take our bodies and businesses outside of London and the southeast.

What do you hope your BFI legacy will be?

I hope people admire the range of films, the clarity and fairness, and that people really understand that I stand for inclusion and access in the various ways one can interpret what that means. And that I showed up. I felt I put a lot of time into being in person at events, not just in London and the southeast, but around the country, internationally.

People often commented, “I didn’t expect to see you here; I thought you’d be too busy or too grand.” I don’t want to ever be either one of those things.

article_text:
Bruno Santamaría Razo’s fiction debut “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”(“Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul”) has clinched the top Ojo award at the 24 th Morelia Film Festival (FICM), which wraps Oct. 25.

Hailed by Variety as a “lush, poetic film rooted in memories,” it became the first Mexican feature to compete at Cannes’ Critics Week in 20 years.

Morelia’s international jury, led by J.A. Bayona (“Society of the Snow”), praised the coming-of-age film for “courageously exploring the past, embracing pain and transforming it …into an expression of pure, unbound beauty.”

Drawing on the filmmaker’s own experiences, the drama traces back to a defining moment in his childhood: the year he turned eleven and when his father was diagnosed with HIV.

“Six Months…” also nabbed the Audience Award for fiction films, a strong indication of its box office potential.

Alejandro Ramírez, Cinépolis CEO and FICM president, described the festival’s 24th edition as a particularly Mexican celebration as it welcomed some of Mexico’s finest filmmakers and actors, including Guillermo del Toro , Alfonso Cuarón , Carlos Reygadas, Jonás Cuarón, Diego Luna , Gael García Bernal, Demián Bichir, Diego Boneta and Luis Gerardo Méndez.

With James Gray in town to present his crime drama “Paper Tiger” and J.A. Bayona serving as jury president, the festival has enjoyed a standout edition, he noted. Bayona also presented “Beyond Society,” a three-part documentary about the making of “Society of the Snow.”

“I think the films this year represent the wide diversity of Mexican cinematic imagination,” festival director Daniel Michel observed.

“There are many different and fascinating stories covering the breadth of experiences in our country which, we hope, will find a home in cinemas, as well as a large spectatorship. We’re also very proud to represent very different regions; Mexico is not a country one can easily summarize, but, rather, a vast territory with many differences which, I believe, our official selection has tried to gather in a single place.”

Meanwhile, Joaquin del Paso’s “The Garden We Dreamed,” which turns on a Haitian family traveling north in search of a better future, snagged two awards: a Special Mention and Best Cinematography for its DP, Gökhan Tiryaki.

“Sad Girlz,” a buzz film at the fest, was recognized as the best fiction debut with the Casa Wabis-Escine award, lauded by the jury for its “genuine performances” and “impeccable exploration of a young modern teen’s life, with all its complexities and contradictions.”

The rest of the awards were quite evenly distributed. Santiago Maza, whose “Black Shine” competed among the short films , won the ECAM award, a scholarship for a Master’s degree in distribution from the prestigious Madrid Film School (ECAM).

Nicolas Pereda snapped up the Best Director award with his a bsurdist comedy “Everything Else Is Noise,” which also snagged his lead Teresa Sanchez (“Flies”) a Best Actress Ojo prize for her performance as Tere, a cello musician-composer in whose apartment her colleague Rosa arranges her first television interview.

Sam Louwyck won the Best Actor prize for his portrayal of a gay hairdresser in Nathalia Acevedo’s “Beauty Salon,” where his salon serves as a refuge for marginalized people.

Noted Michel: “We’re also very pleased to have had directors from very different backgrounds and identities who have brought their perspectives and very singular ideas on filmmaking to our festival.”

Next year, the festival will be moving its dates back to the last week before the Day of the Dead. FICM is already gearing up for its 25th anniversary, promising a landmark edition with major guests, bold retrospectives and a stellar lineup.

Among the highlights of the 10-day festival:

“ Naza ”

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary “Naza” – which means collateral damage – played to a packed Teatro Matamoros after which it unsurprisingly won an audience award. Unlike its reception at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, where it won the Special Jury Prize and received a record-breaking standing ovation, it was met with stunned silence as the credits rolled.

Presenting the documentary beforehand was festival VP Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Batel who underscored the importance of the screening to help audiences understand such a complex conflict. He noted that the Israeli filmmakers have been unable to return to their country after being accused of treason, adding that such accusations by a “criminal government” are a source of pride for those working toward peaceful solutions.

He reaffirmed the festival’s commitment to peace, dialogue and ending violence worldwide, calling for an end to the ongoing genocide against the Palestinian people.

Film critic Alonso Díaz de la Vega, also spoke, describing Naza as a “deeply moving” film that exposes not only the genocide in Gaza but also the global implications of military technology, artificial intelligence and surveillance.

“The most important thing this screening can inspire is not silence, but the words ‘Free Palestine,’” Díaz de la Vega concluded. The film opens in select theaters in Mexico on Oct. 22.

Guillermo del Toro Rules

At the festival to present the 3D re-release of his much-lauded “Pan’s Labyrinth,” the anti-authoritarian theme of his Oscar-winning fable hit home even harder this time, given the rise of right-wing governments across the region and the world at large.

Speaking to hordes of mostly young fans at his Masterclass and later at a press conference and multiple one-on-one interviews, the indefatigable filmmaker reflected on the current state of affairs in the world.

He grew emotional at the presser when he said: “The state of our species and society today goes beyond anything we could have imagined back then. But I recognize the same sadness and despair. It pains me deeply to see one, two, or three generations fail the next. We’re handing down a world in ruins, morally, socially and spiritually fractured, with the very fabric that once allowed us to tell fables and parables falling apart.”

French-Mexican Alliance

As part of the partnership established in 2003 between FICM and Cannes Critics’ Week, this year’s edition presented a selection of eight films and one short that screened at the sidebar last May. Ava Cahen, artistic director of the Cannes Film Festival’s parallel section, led the screenings, which included such titles as Aina Clotet’s “Viva,” Alexander Murphy’s “Tin Castle” and Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown.”

Toasting Mexico and France’s 200 years of diplomatic relations this year, French ambassador to Mexico Delphine Borione awarded Alfonso Cuarón the insignia of Officer of the Order of Arts and Letters during the fest to honor his “extraordinary contribution to contemporary cinema, singular vision, artistic reinvention and role in bringing Mexican culture to global audiences.”

Calling Cuarón “one of the greatest filmmakers of our time,” she praised his universal vision and the cultural ties his work has forged between Mexico and France. “To speak to the world, one must never stop being oneself,” she said, reflecting on his films, from “Y Tu Mamá También” to “Roma.”

Reflecting on France’s deep influence on his filmmaking, Cuarón described cinema as “not a narrative art, but a musical art” – a rhythmic, organic creation with its own heartbeat and a direct image of time.

He closed by addressing France’s current political turmoil, expressing hope that young people’s calls for change would be heard rather than co-opted by opportunism. Quoting French writer Pascal Quignard, he concluded: “I do not believe art can ever be negative. It ignores negation because it ignores time.”

article_text:
British filmmaker Joanna Hogg , who has been serving as president of the Feature Narrative Competition jury at the ninth edition of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival this week, tells Variety she prefers to know as little as possible about a film before watching it, “not even a synopsis of the story.”

“I prefer to go in with no criteria and a very open mind,” she explains. “I am looking for something that moves me, but it also can be something that strikes me in a particular way. It doesn’t have to reduce me to tears, but just something that’s maybe got a clarity about it, a feeling that the filmmaker has ideas and a vision.”

Related Stories

'The Simpsons' Surprise: Apu Is Heard for the First Time in Nearly a Decade, as Sunil Malhotra Takes Over for Hank Azaria (EXCLUSIVE)

With films from both first-time and established directors, a range of genres and stories from different parts of the world, Hogg sees little sense in applying the same criteria to each. “I really feel like I’ve travelled, even though I’ve been here in El Gouna. I’ve really travelled all over the place.”

It is Hogg’s first visit to Egypt, and she describes herself as something of an outsider on a jury that includes filmmakers from Egypt, Iraq and Turkey. Listening to their perspectives, she notes, has “inspired me to discover films, actually not just from Egypt, but the Middle East in general.”

The experience also marks a return to watching films after months spent largely immersed in her own writing. “I’ve been stuck at home for quite a few months writing and actually not watching any films,” Hogg explains. “It’s been really nice to come here with a sort of clear mind, not having been watching cinema at all. Reading a lot, but not watching. And so I think it made me more receptive to the films.”

Hogg is currently writing her next film, which once again has her grappling with the line between lived experience and fiction. The director’s work, which includes “The Souvenir,” “The Souvenir Part II” and “The Eternal Daughter,” is deeply personal.

“I’m very interested in the sort of tension between what’s personal and a real experience that I’ve had and turning that into cinema and into fiction,” she goes on.

Despite drawing on her own experiences across several films, Hogg doesn’t feel the process has become any easier. “It’s a different story that I’m telling with this film. Each time I’m learning from scratch in a way, which I quite like,” she says.

Hogg graduated from film school, but found herself working in television rather than making films, an experience she remembers with little fondness.

“It was a disappointment in a way that I went into television,” she acknowledges. “I went into it because I needed to work and it wasn’t as easy as I thought making a first feature film.”

The turning point came, she remembers, while she was directing a television episode to which she felt little connection. “I almost can remember where I was standing when I thought this,” Hogg recalls. “I was rehearsing a scene with these actors. It was very much television and it was not a story that I had any relationship to. I hadn’t written the script.”

Her realization was simple. “I thought, I really must tell something personal.”

The late American film producer Barbara Stone, a friend of Hogg’s who would go on to produce “Unrelated,” her 2007 debut film, supplied the final push. When Hogg told her she intended to make a short, Stone challenged her, asking, “Why make a short film? Make a feature.”

Hogg’s working relationship, and friendship, with Tilda Swinton dates back even further, to her 1986 graduation film, “Caprice.” Their career paths diverged creatively for decades before they reunited on “The Souvenir” films and later “The Eternal Daughter.”

“We talk about this sometimes and we said, ‘Well, actually, maybe it’s not a bad thing. We both developed our own way first,’” Hogg reflects. “Then when we came together with ‘The Souvenir,’ which was many years later, it was such a pleasure. We did think, well, ‘Why the hell have we taken this long to do another piece of work? We’ll do more work together.’”

For now, however, Hogg’s attention is on the still-unannounced film waiting for her back home. After days immersed in the work of other filmmakers at El Gouna, she anticipates some difficulty returning to the world of her own film.

“I’ll have to decompress,” she explains, allowing the films she has been watching to settle before she can “come quietly back to my story.”

WPA Murals at Harlem Hospital Restored to Their Original Glory

A New Deal-era sculpture by John Rhoden was also included in the city's restoration project.

NYC Health + Hospitals’ Arts in Medicine department wrapped up conservation work on three New Deal-era murals and a John Rhoden sculpture held at its Harlem hospital on Wednesday, October 14.

Located in the hospital's indoor mural pavilion, the Great Depression-era works were made during a pivotal period in United States history when Black artists advocated for and gained unprecedented access to major public commissions through the Works Progress Administration 's (WPA) Federal Art Project . Among the commissioned works were Charles Alston's two companion murals, "Magic in Medicine" (1940) and "Modern Medicine (1940)," and Hayes's eight-panel mural, "Pursuit of Happiness" (1937), which have been restored as part of the preservation effort in Harlem.

"In 1936, when these designs were submitted, administrators at the time objected to them because they said there was 'too much black subject matter,'" Larissa Trinder, head of the Arts in Medicine program, told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. After artists publicly protested the verdict, the hospital commissioner reversed the decision .

article_text:
Bill Hader has always wanted to direct a feature film . It’s just taken him a while to get to it.

“That was the dream forever. I just took the most circuitous way to get there,” Hader said. Then he cracked, “I think Kurosawa did that? Didn’t he go to a sketch comedy show for eight years? Wasn’t he in ‘Trainwreck’?”

After a long tenure on “Saturday Night Live,” starring roles in several films and co-creating his own Emmy-winning HBO series “Barry,” Hader finally got around to directing his own movie, “ They Know .” In a one-on-one conversation called “What No One Tells You About Directing Your First Feature,” Hader unpacked exactly that for the audience at IndieWire ‘s Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit presented by AT&T in Los Angeles on Saturday.

With “They Know,” Hader is the latest major comedic talent to make the jump to the horror genre. As he did on “Barry,” Hader writes, directs and acts in the feature. He stars as a divorced father who begins to suspect that his ex-wife’s secret new partner is having an unorthodox effect on his children. The MRC-produced film, which also stars Linda Cardellini, wrapped photography in May and is currently in the sound-mixing stage and prepping to show to distributors.

Hader shared that the premise for the film came about from personal conversations he had with his longtime collaborator and writing partner, Duffy Boudreau.

“We’re both divorced. We were talking about how lucky we were that we were on, like, we had really good terms with our ex-wives, and we have kids with them,” Hader told Chris O’Falt, IndieWire’s VP of features strategy and host of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “We started talking about the worst case scenarios of, ‘Oh, my god, this person is going through this and this person is going through that.’ And then this idea came up.”

While keeping the plot details vague, Hader admitted that he “kind of gave up on” the film for a while, as the ending of each draft felt “like every other horror movie.” But a curious new release in 2025, about the unsavory world of online scalpers, finally tipped him back towards the project.

“I went to the Nuart [Theater] by myself and I saw the movie ‘Cloud,’ by Kiyoshi Kurosawa,” he said. “And, [my movie] is nothing like that movie. But, for some reason, I saw that movie and I walked out and I was like, ‘I think I know how to do it.’ You would never see this movie and think ‘Cloud,’ but that’s where it’s at.”

A feature project has been long in the works for Hader, one of the most conspicuous cinephiles to emerge from the cast of “SNL.” (Check his second visit to the Criterion Closet , in which he pulls a whopping 15 titles — including Robert Bresson’s “A Man Escaped,” “Salvatore Giuliano” and an Allan King box set.) After helming many episodes of “Barry” — and earning a Directors Guild of America award in 2019 for the series — a push into feature filmmaking has seemed inevitable for several years.

Nonetheless, Hader maintains that he was carrying some self-doubt heading into the project, something he’s had since his sketch comedy days.

“‘SNL’ helped with that. You would just get shot down constantly. It was horrible,” Hader said with a smile. “But, in doing that, you are working on instinct.”

That healthy amount of fear helped Hader foster collaborative conversations throughout the filmmaking process, whether it was testing the looks of different lenses on location scouts or talking through his shot lists with his editor in pre-production.

“The doubt is always there. And that’s good though. If you’re not scared, then you’re fucked,” Hader said. “I met someone who worked with [Martin] Scorsese. He said the best thing about it was that he would start a day and go, ‘I don’t know what I’m doing. I don’t know what this is.’ And that’s just freeing. … We’re all scared. The worst is when people come in like, ‘I know what’s going on.’ And within five minutes you’re like, ‘The director doesn’t know what they’re doing.'”

Hader returned to the sentiment in the home-stretch of the conversation, underlining the takeaway to the crowd.

“Don’t be afraid to be wrong. That’s the thing that screwed me up. I was so terrified of looking like an idiot,” he said. “Be wrong as fast as you can be. Like, this is all wrong, but it doesn’t matter. We’re just going to. We’re going to be OK. Just keep moving.”

Along with Hader’s “What No One Tells You About Directing Your First Feature” presentation, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit also included a keynote by directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller, diving into the production of their sci-fi blockbuster “Project Hail Mary,” and an appearance by “Obsession” writer/director Curry Barker, who was presented with IndieWire’s inaugural Future of Filmmaking award.

Watch the complete conversation with Hader in the video above.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen. For more information, visit here .

article_text:
Tre uomini con il volto coperto hanno fatto irruzione nella serata del 27 ottobre nella Galleria Rosso20sette di Roma , dove è in corso The Collapse of Democracy – States of Injustice, Chapter 2 , mostra personale della street artist Laika . Gli aggressori hanno minacciato e immobilizzato il gallerista Stefano Ferraro e imbrattato con vernice spray nera le opere esposte. Sul posto è intervenuta la polizia e sono in corso le indagini per identificare i responsabili e chiarire la matrice dell’azione.

Secondo le prime ricostruzioni, al momento dell’irruzione Ferraro era solo all’interno dello spazio di via del Sudario 39. Gli uomini lo avrebbero bloccato e minacciato prima di intervenire sulle opere. La galleria non dispone di un sistema di videosorveglianza interno ma sono presenti telecamere nella strada e un testimone avrebbe assistito alla scena dall’esterno.

The Collapse of Democracy, dagli Stati Uniti a Roma

The Collapse of Democracy – States of Injustice, Chapter 2 sviluppa una ricerca avviata da Laika negli Stati Uniti e incentrata sulle contraddizioni della società e della politica americana contemporanea. Le opere affrontano i temi del razzismo, delle disuguaglianze, del diritto all’aborto, della diffusione delle armi, della pena di morte e della questione palestinese attraverso il linguaggio diretto che caratterizza la produzione dell’artista, conosciuta soprattutto per poster e interventi realizzati nello spazio pubblico.

L’esposizione comprende una ventina di lavori tra tele, opere su carta e installazioni. Tra questi figurano The King is Naked , con Donald Trump raffigurato nudo, Burn, Tesla, Burn , un’immagine di una Tesla in fiamme, e un lavoro nel quale Patti Smith rivendica «Free Palestine». Altre opere richiamano figure della lotta contro il razzismo come Rosa Parks e Martin Luther King .

Laika: «Non mi avete fatto paura»

Laika ha definito l’episodio un tentativo di intimidazione e censura politica. In un messaggio diffuso dopo l’aggressione, l’artista ha collegato quanto accaduto a quello che considera un clima più generale di violenza e repressione e ha definito l’azione «Di stampo squadrista». L’identità degli aggressori e la matrice del raid devono ancora essere accertate dagli investigatori.

«Questi ragazzi incappucciati hanno tentato di censurarmi e mettermi paura. Non solo non ci siete riusciti, ma mi avete convinto che la mia arte non solo dà fastidio ed è efficace», ha dichiarato Laika, annunciando di voler continuare a utilizzare il proprio lavoro per affrontare temi come fascismo, razzismo, xenofobia, omofobia, violenza di genere e guerra a Gaza.

Laika aveva già ricevuto minacce attraverso i social network e alcune sue opere nello spazio pubblico erano state danneggiate o rimosse ma quello alla Rosso20sette rappresenta il primo episodio in cui l’azione contro il suo lavoro è stata accompagnata da un’aggressione fisica all’interno di uno spazio espositivo.

Le reazioni politiche

L’episodio ha suscitato diverse reazioni. Giovanni Barbera , segretario della federazione di Roma, Castelli e Litoranea di Rifondazione Comunista e membro della direzione nazionale del partito, ha espresso solidarietà a Laika e al gallerista, definendo l’azione un’intimidazione che richiama «Pratiche squadriste».

Barbera ha chiesto al ministro dell’Interno Matteo Piantedosi di verificare le attività delle organizzazioni neofasciste e, nei casi previsti dalla legge, di intervenire attraverso gli strumenti già contemplati dall’ordinamento. Anche in questo caso, il riferimento alla matrice neofascista rappresenta una valutazione politica: saranno gli inquirenti a stabilire identità e motivazioni degli aggressori.

È intervenuta anche Marilena Grassadonia , coordinatrice delle politiche per i diritti LGBT+ di Roma Capitale, che ha definito l’accaduto «un gesto vigliacco e squadrista» e ha ricordato alcuni degli interventi realizzati da Laika negli ultimi anni nella Capitale, tra cui le opere dedicate a Maja T. e Michela Murgia .

«Nessun segno nero potrà mai cancellare la libertà dell’arte», ha dichiarato Grassadonia, esprimendo solidarietà all’artista.

article_text:
President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday seeking to designate the Oval Office and the adjacent Cabinet Room national monuments, saying that the new designation would prevent future administrations from making major modifications without Congressional approval. In his second term, Trump made it a priority to redecorate both, turning the previously restrained presidential working spaces into extravagantly gilded interiors in the style of Louis XIV.

In the immediate aftermath of this week’s midterm elections, in which his party suffered historic defeats, Trump appeared to be self-soothing by focusing on the many renovation projects he has initiated at the White House and across Washington, D.C. At the White House, in addition to his makeover of the Oval Office, these have included the construction of a granite helipad on the White House’s South Lawn and, most notoriously, the demolition of the building’s East Wing to make way for a 90,000-square-foot, $600 million ballroom. (On Wednesday, in his first public appearance after Tuesday’s Republican wipeout, Trump led a media tour of the ballroom construction site.)

Around the nation’s capital, Trump has embarked on a fraught, $14 million repair of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, begun the redevelopment of a popular public golf course by cutting down hundreds of trees, and proposed a 250-foot-high triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Apparently worried that incoming Democrats would block construction of the arch, Trump asked for hastened approval of the project, which was granted Wednesday by his hand-picked planning commission; that evening, Judge Tanya Chutkan stopped construction for fourteen days.

It is not clear how designating the Oval Office a national monument will prevent another president from simply revising, or ignoring, the designation—the White House itself is already designated a national historic landmark, which has not stopped Trump from building his ballroom. Nevertheless, speaking from the now gold-saturated Oval Office, Trump told reporters, “When completed, and when we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it’ll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space.”

2026 wird zum 13. Mal der Siegfried Kracauer Preis für die beste deutschsprachige Filmkritik des Jahres vergeben. Zu den fünf nominierten Texten zählt auch die Filmdienst-Rezension zu „Dry Leaf“ von Esther Buss. Mit dem Preis für die „Beste innovative Form der Filmkritik“ wird das vierköpfige Autorenteam einer Podcast-Serie über Werner Herzog ausgezeichnet.

Seit 2014 wird jährlich der Siegfried Kracauer Preis an Filmkritikerinnen und Filmkritiker vergeben. Schon zum 13. Mal zeichnen die MFG Filmförderung Baden-Württemberg, die Film- und Medienstiftung NRW und die Mitteldeutsche Medienförderung (MDM) in Zusammenarbeit mit dem Verband der deutschen Filmkritik die beste deutschsprachige Filmkritik aus. Am 27. Oktober wurden die fünf Nominierten bekanntgegeben, die eine dreiköpfige Fachjury – bestehend aus der Kinoleiterin Ulrike Schüler, dem Leiter des Frankfurter Lichter Filmfests Gregor Maria Schubert und der Filmkritikerin und Vorjahresgewinnerin Rahel Jung – unter 83 eingereichten Texten ausgewählt hat.

Fünf Texte sind die Kandidaten

Eine der fünf nominierten Kritiken ist auf filmdienst.de erschienen: Die Rezension von Esther Buss zu „ Dry Leaf “ von Alexandre Koberidze, einem in hypnotischer Langsamkeit gefilmten Road Movie über die Suche nach einer verschwundenen Fotografin in Georgien, der sich viel Zeit für magisch-realistische Abschweifungen nimmt. Ebenfalls nominiert wurden die Besprechung von Mathis Raabe zu der Stephen-King-Verfilmung „The Long Walk“ auf zeit.de ( hier nachzulesen ) sowie drei Rezensionen, die auf der Online-Plattform critic.de erschienen: Annette Brauerhoch für die Kritik zum feministischen Filmklassiker „Wanda“ ( hier nachzulesen ), Sonja M. Schultz für die Rezension zum Dokumentarfilm „Kommunist“ ( hier nachzulesen ) über den ehemaligen DDR-Staatschef Egon Krenz und Lukas Stern für die Besprechung von Adrian Goigingers Trauerdrama „Vier minus Drei“ ( hier nachzulesen ).

Die Gewinnerin oder der Gewinner der mit 5000 Euro dotierten Auszeichnung wird am 3. November im Rahmen des Kinoprogrammpreis NRW in der Wolkenburg Köln bekanntgegeben. Bereits entschieden ist, wer 2026 den zum dritten Mal vergebenen Siegfried Kracauer Preis für die „Beste Innovative Form der Filmkritik“ erhält, die ebenfalls mit 5000 Euro dotiert ist. Die Jury wählte das vierköpfige Autoren-Team Max Osenstätter (auch Moderator), Klaus Uhrig (auch Produzent), Judith Goetsch und Johannes Munzinger der sechsteiligen Podcast-Serie „ Werner Herzog – zu groß für Deutschland “ von SWR Kultur aus. Die Jury lobte die Produktion als hochwertig und hob hervor, dass der Podcast gerade für ein jüngeres Publikum eine spannende und abwechslungsreiche Erzählweise finde.

Weekly News Roundup: November 2, 2026

Art Basel Qatar Names Participants For 2027 Edition

Art Basel Qatar has announced 82 galleries from 37 countries and territories for its second edition, slated to run from January 28–30 in Msheireb Downtown Doha. 30 exhibitors are newcomers, including Jhaveri Contemporary, Richard Saltoun, and Hanart TZ Gallery, while returning exhibitors include Gagosian, Perrotin, David Zwirner, Nature Morte, and Axel Vervoordt. The tally is down slightly from the inaugural edition’s 87, with Hauser & Wirth and Pace Gallery opting not to return as the region faces renewed geopolitical uncertainty. Each gallery will mount a solo-artist presentation responding to the theme “between / بين,” conceived by Iraqi curator Wassan Al-Khudhairi. In a statement, she describes it as a “liminal space of possibility, where different perspectives, histories, and ideas meet and new ways of seeing emerge.”

HONG JIN-HWON . Courtesy the artist.

Hong Jin-hwon Wins Korea Artist Prize 2026

Photojournalist-turned-artist Hong Jin-hwon has been awarded the Korea Artist Prize 2026 by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA Seoul). Announced on October 28, the prize recognizes his use of photography, video, and web programming to examine how political struggle is staged and circulated as imagery. His new video The Highest Form of the Image Is Armed Struggle (2026) sets the rhetoric of past revolutionary movements against scenes from present-day South Korean rallies. Charmaine Toh, acting head of curatorial at Tate Modern and a member of the six-person jury, said the work reveals how tensions are “represented as images, and questions the visual systems through which we see and understand reality.” Hong was chosen from four finalists, whose works, including those of Lee Hai Min Sun, Lee Jung-woo, and Jeon Hyun-sun, are on view at MMCA Seoul through December 6.

Nolan Jimbo Joins Whitney Museum as Arnhold Associate Curator

The Whitney Museum of American Art in New York has appointed Nolan Jimbo as its Arnhold associate curator, effective November 16, succeeding Rujeko Hockley. Jimbo, who specializes in Asian diasporic artists, is currently assistant curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. During his five-year tenure there, he organized two collection exhibitions and various solo shows for artists such as Kenzi Shiokava (2026) and Gregory Bae (2022). He also co-directed the MCA DNA Research Initiative, a multiyear program dedicated to studying the museum’s collection and archives, and held curatorial positions at the Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art and the Dallas Museum of Art. At the Whitney, he will oversee exhibitions and public programs. In a statement, Jimbo noted, “I look forward to building upon [the Whitney’s] legacy while advocating for emerging and overlooked artistic practices, particularly at this moment when the museum is attracting ever younger and more diverse audiences.”

Irini Papadimitriou Tapped to Lead 14th Seoul Mediacity Biennale

The Seoul Museum of Art has appointed Irini Papadimitriou as artistic director of the 14th Seoul Mediacity Biennale, set to open in August 2027. The forthcoming exhibition, titled “Machines of Repair,” will examine how societies, power systems, and art are impacted by emerging technologies. Currently director of exhibitions at Diriyah Art Futures in Riyadh, Papadimitriou previously worked at London’s V&A and Manchester’s FutureEverything. She also served as artistic director of the 2023 Busan Sea Art Festival. In a press release, she remarked, “At a time when technological innovation is too often driven by conquest, extraction, surveillance, and control, . . . my vision is to open up a space for collective imagination and dialogue, asking how technology might be reoriented towards infrastructures of the public good.

Harrie Fasher Wins 2026 Sculpture by the Sea Prize New South Wales-based artist Harrie Fasher received the AUD 70,000 (USD 49,200) Aqualand Sculpture Award for Unveiling the Edges of the Sky (2026), currently on display at Sydney’s annual Sculpture by the Sea. Fasher, who is renowned for her large-scale installations and small-format works, is the fourth woman to win the prize in its 30-year history. A six-by-five-meter web-like construction of steel, bronze, and timber, Unveiling explores female strength, intuition, and the disintegration of the ego. The abstract sculpture joins 99 others made by local and international artists at this year’s edition , spanning two kilometers of the Bondi to Tamarama Beach Walk and Marks Park. The outdoor exhibition remains open to the public through November 2.

article_text:
John Turturro and cinematographer Sam Levy hadn’t worked together before, both signing onto Noah Segan’s “ The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, ” but they did have something in common. Levy came up as a camera assistant under the great Harris Savides , who also shot Turturro in “Margot at the Wedding.” They’d both gotten close to Savides and had all kinds of stories that gave the actor and DP a nice shared language to work on this throwback crime thriller about a thief named Harry (Turturro) who steals from the wrong vape goon (Will Price) and has one last, desperate chance to make good.

But Levy also had something tangible.

“ The Only Living Pickpocket in New York ” was shot primarily with a set of Bausch & Lomb Super Baltar lenses — the same set, in fact, that cinematographer Gordon Willis used to shoot “The Godfather.” But Savides also owned an even older set of original Baltar lenses that Levy brought to bless the set. “I carried Harris’ lenses with us,” Levy told IndieWire. “They’re very similar but had just a little bit of a different flavor, and they had a different focal length. Some of them had kind of in-between focal lengths. So, it was convenient, but it also just felt nice to have a piece of Harris.”

It’s especially nice for the eyes of the project, the lenses, to have history and lineage on a movie like “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York.” Segan’s thriller takes as its central dramatic question the tension between the analog and the digital, the New York that’s coming into being in the 2020s and the New York that’s disintegrating to bring it to life. And Levy really wanted to lean into that, visually.

“[The Super Baltars] have these aberrations in them which put off a lot of people. They vignette and they flare in a way that is very beautiful but you can’t — it’s hard [to control. For example, if you shoot with the iris wide open, they completely fall apart, and they look soft, but not in a pleasing way. Harris Savides used them on ‘Margot at the Wedding,’ which John is in. And at that time, I remember having a lot of conversations with [Savides] about how difficult they were,” Levy said.

But after doing some camera tests with Turturro and seeing how he looked through those lenses, Levy found a sweet spot that’s weathered and alluring, with a clarity that is purposeful but never too sharp or soulless. The flaws and the aberrations the lenses created were, in fact, Levy’s favorite parts. “It’s an urgent necessity to take risks when you’re a cinematographer and to try things that are maybe on the edge of being too dark or underexposed. I played a lot with that in this film , with silhouette,” Levy said.

This is especially true in the Bronx apartment that Harry shares with his wife Rosie (Karina Arroyave), trapped in a hospital bed in what New Yorker realtors would call a “prewar” building and what most New Yorkers would call “don’t trust that elevator to work.” Levy spent a lot of time there, trying to see and absorb the character of the space, not to correct it with lighting, but to see how it could help tell the story through how his camera captured it.

“ You open the door, you see the hallway; you close the door, it’s completely dark, and I knew so much happens in that little stretch. And I had to really spend time there to get to a place where it’s like, ‘Oh, when he comes home, he’ll emerge out of the darkness,” Levy said.

Levy also worked with production designer Rocío Giménez to arrange the space so we felt the transition and the invasion of Harry’s home when it happens. How can that conflict pop in the frame before the actors even start speaking?

“I suggested, ‘Why don’t we put a picture up and we see the guys in the reflection?’” Levy said. “It’s got to be at a very particular angle, and then we’ve got to light them so that you can really see [the goons in the next room], but we’re panning from John. It really was all in one. So that was really fun, but it was very painstaking to plot that out, and I worked very closely with Rocío Giménez, our great production designer, and our art director, Rosa Callejas, on being able to get that,” Levy said.

Giménez told IndieWire that her goal was to make sure Harry and Rosie’s apartment reflected a home that had history, and therefore room for all those hidden surprise angles, too. “It needed to feel textured — in the objects, in the layers of paint — and never remodeled. Things break, walls chip, and those marks accumulate over time. We also wanted the apartment to feel very warm, almost glowing. Although the apartment was a location, we transformed it extensively: reworking parts of the kitchen, adding wallpaper, repainting, and building walls to make the space feel smaller,” Giménez said.

Giménez and her team also made adjustments to make the home invasion look properly invasive, scattering even more objects around every time we cut back to it. But it took a real team effort to craft that sense of lived history that imbues every frame of “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” and especially those sequences in Harry’s apartment. Giménez, Levy, and Segan all talked about it extensively, and then, at a certain point, let their New York location have its say, too.

“When you’re working on a location — sometimes you don’t have the time, but it takes time to acclimate to the environment. And one thing I really learned from Harris Savides, that he would always say to me when, a few times, I got to operate for him, ‘Just look. Take a look at what you’re doing. Look at it. Don’t frame it up. Just sit there and look,’” Levy said.

It’s apt, then, that Savides’ lenses were on Turturro, right alongside Levy’s.

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” is now playing in theaters.

article_text:
Questions have been raised over the maintenance of Taliesin West, Frank Lloyd Wright ’s former home and studio, after a visitor was reportedly struck and killed on October 16 by an acrylic fragment that had been dislodged from the property by high winds.

The Scottsdale Police Department has identified the deceased as Brazilian national Rogério Renato Mateucci, rector of the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná, who had traveled to the US for an event at Arizona State University. According to authorities, Mateucci was struck by a roof piece during a walking tour. Mateucci was pronounced dead at the scene.

The National Weather Service reported east winds of 22 miles per hour in the area of Scottsdale with gusts up to 32 miles per hour, on October 16, and people were warned that travel or safety may be disrupted as a result.

In a statement, Joe Spector, the chief executive of the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation, said that the foundation “extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of the individual” and that “no further details will be shared out of respect for privacy and to allow officials to complete their work.” Authorities are treating Mateucci’s death as a weather-related accident, further investigating pending.

Whether his death was preventable, however, has been questioned in the days since.

Vidal Martins, a colleague of Mateucci who identified his body from photographs, told The Arizona Public , that “security measures must be taken because it’s a public place.” He also shared a photo of a translucent panel lying among rocks and desert vegetation outside Taliesin West.

A former employee has also spoken out on the topic, telling local news channel AZ Family on the condition of anonymity that they had witnessed two other objects breaking loose from the roof, as well as a similar panel coming loose during a monsoon over the summer. The source claimed that “money [isn’t] being funneled into the proper channels to ensure that the building is safe.” The property has temporarily closed without a date for reopening in place yet.

ARTnews has contacted the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation for comment.

Wright built the studio and home in 1937 and lived there until his death in 1959. The property spans across 491 acres, and in 1986 opened as the Frank Lloyd Wright School of Architecture, before changing its name to The School of Architecture.

Natürlich fehlen auch die klassischen Motive nicht: der Munot, die St.-Johann-Kirche oder der Fronwagplatz. Doch selbst diese vertrauten Ansichten erscheinen bei Beat Wolf oft überraschend anders. Er hat ein ausgeprägtes Gespür für ungewöhnliche Perspektiven und sorgfältig austarierte Bildkompositionen. Linien, Formen und architektonische Elemente fügt er zu harmonischen Bildausschnitten zusammen, die selbst altbekannte Sehenswürdigkeiten in neuem Licht erscheinen lassen.

Auf diesem Spaziergang durch die Altstadt ist auch Max Baumann mit dabei – mit seinem sehr lesenswerten Text. Während Beat Wolf das heutige Schaffhausen mit seiner Kamera erkundet, lässt Baumann die Stadt vergangener Jahrzehnte wieder aufleben. Er erinnert an die Zeit nach der Bombardierung Schaffhausens, an prachtvolle Altstadtbauten, die dem Zahn der Zeit zum Opfer fielen und durch weniger Schönes ersetzt wurden. Oder an jene Jahre, als sich noch ganze Fahrzeugkolonnen durch die Vordergasse quälten, verzweifelt nach einem Parkplatz suchten und schliesslich vielleicht auf dem Mosergarten fündig wurden …

Beat Wolf hat sein Vorhaben, ein neues fotografisches Buch über Schaffhausen zu schaffen, auf überzeugende Weise verwirklicht. Dabei ist weit mehr entstanden als eine Sammlung schöner Stadtansichten. Immer wieder überrascht er mit kreativen Bildideen, die über die klassische Architekturfotografie hinausgehen: etwa mit seinen freischwebenden Erkern, einer originellen Sammlung von Wirtshausschildern und Kaminen oder ungewöhnlichen Aussichten aus der Hundeperspektive. Und da und dort entdeckt man in seinen Fotografien kleine Details, die sich bei genauerem Hinsehen als humorvolle Pointen entpuppen.

Beat Wolf fotografiert Schaffhausen nicht mit dem neugierigen Blick eines Besuchers, sondern mit der Vertrautheit eines Menschen, der seine Stadt seit Jahrzehnten kennt – und dennoch immer wieder Neues in ihr entdeckt. Sein fotografischer Spaziergang ist deshalb nicht nur ein schönes Stadtporträt, sondern auch eine Einladung, genauer hinzusehen und selbst dort Überraschendes zu entdecken, wo man schon unzählige Male vorbeigegangen ist.

Für wen ist dieses Buch? Ganz klar: Für alle, die Schaffhausen kennen, kennenlernen oder in Erinnerung behalten möchten. Da sind zunächst die Schaffhauser selbst, für die dieser Bildband ein originelles Coffee-Table-Book sein dürfte. Dann die Touristen, die ein besonderes Stück Stadterlebnis mit nach Hause nehmen möchten. Und schliesslich die Heimweh-Schaffhauser, die wohl immer wieder darin blättern werden, um sich gedanklich in ihre liebste Stadt zurückzuversetzen.

Urs Tillmanns

Der Rundgang beginnt auf der uralten Handelsstrasse von der Unterstadt bis zum Obertor, also dem Rückgrat der Stadt ums Jahr 1000 mit der alten Stadtkirche St. Johann. Der Fotograf

Beat Wolf (*1952) wuchs in der Schaffhauser Altstadt auf und absolvierte eine Lehre als Hochbauzeichner. Er fotografiert seit 1974, interessiert sich für alte Musikinstrumente und eröffnete 1976 als Autodidakt sein eigenes Atelier für den Bau und die Restaurierung historischer Musikinstrumente, was ihn dazu bewegt bei verschiedenen Ensembles mitzuwirken. Source: Shutterstock

Michael B. Jordan at 2026 Actor Awards

Amazon MGM Studios is making a major move into France’s theatrical distribution market, with the release of Michael B. Jordan’s reimagining of The Thomas Crown Affair under its own banner on March 3, 2027.

The film, directed by and starring Jordan alongside Kenneth Branagh and Adria Arjona, had previously been scheduled for release through Sony Pictures Entertainment France under the companies’ international distribution agreement. It will retain its original release date, including Imax screenings.

The move marks a significant step in Amazon MGM’s expansion into French theatrical distribution, as the studio begins handling its own releases.

The company has also dated The Haunting Of Hotel Transylvania , the fifth instalment in the Sony Pictures Animation franchise, for October 6, 2027.

Amazon MGM Studios’ French distribution operation is led by joint heads of territory Lucie Trampoglieri (head of distribution) and Marion Pistoresi (head of marketing). The company continues to build its local team as part of a wider push into international theatrical distribution for its feature slate.

Under France’s tightly regulated media chronology, which determines when films can move from cinemas to streaming platforms, Prime Video can make theatrical releases available after a 17-month window, meaning The Thomas Crown Affair could arrive on the service in France from August 2028, subject to applicable conditions and release strategy.

Sony has previously handled local distribution for several Amazon MGM titles in France, including Mercy , Project Hail Mary and Verity , under the international distribution partnership established in 2025. Sony will also release David Leitch’s How To Rob A Bank in France on November 11 before Amazon MGM Studios takes over its upcoming theatrical releases in the territory.

Amazon MGM Studios is opening territory offices in a staggered pattern under the purview of head of international theatrical distribution, Helen Moss, and head of international theatrical marketing, Charlie Coleman. Once it opens an office, Sony will cease to distribute for Amazon MGM Studios in that territory.

Jordan’s The Thomas Crown Affair is a fresh take on Norman Jewison’s 1968 heist thriller starring Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway. Jordan plays a suave art thief who becomes romantically involved with a former FBI agent turned insurance investigator (Arjona) pursuing him, while a sinister adversary (Branagh) threatens to bring him down.

The film is scheduled for release in UK cinemas on March 4 through Amazon MGM Studios, followed by a US release through Amazon MGM Studios on March 5.

Chasing the American dream: How are distributors pitching French films to US audiences?

Reflect , by artist Cannupa Hanska Luger , is the second exhibition presented by For Freedoms at the Corcoran School of the Arts and Design .

Reflect is a living archive of Cannupa Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project , marking ten years since its creation. Rooted in Northern Plains Indigenous traditions, “counting coup” describes an act of courage defined not by violence but by approaching an adversary closely enough to recognize their humanity without causing harm. Luger utilizes this principle as an artistic methodology grounded in proximity, accountability, restraint, and recognition, one that runs throughout Counting Coup: We Are the People , his broader residency encompassing exhibitions, public programs, and community activities.

“Ten years since the creation of a mirror shield and the concept remains relevant. My personal thoughts are that someday it will be forgotten and the need for such devices will become unfathomable,” says Cannupa Hanska Luger.

The Mirror Shield Project was initiated by Luger (Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara, Lakota) in 2016 in support of the Water Protectors at Očhéthi Šakówiŋ (Oceti Sakowin) Camp near Standing Rock, North Dakota. Luger, who grew up on the Standing Rock Reservation, developed the project as an artistic response and a way to mobilize creative communities in solidarity with Indigenous sovereignty and the protection of land and water.

Designed from lightweight, inexpensive, readily available materials, the shields were intentionally easy to reproduce. While an Artist-in-Residence at the Institute of American Indian Arts, Luger worked with Oglala Lakota/Diné filmmaker Razelle Benally to create How to Build Mirror Shields for Water Protectors , an instructional film shared openly through social media. Within weeks, artists, activists, students, families, and anonymous community members across the country created and transported upwards of a thousand mirrored shields to Očhéthi Šakówiŋ Camp, while Water Protectors made additional shields onsite.

From the beginning, Luger imagined the mirrored surfaces not only as a form of protection, but as a way to turn the gaze of surveillance back upon itself. Working with artist Rory Erler Wakemup (Minnesota Chippewa Tribe) and the Water Protector community at Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, hundreds of shields were brought together in a large-scale action in which Water Protectors moved through the camp holding mirrors overhead, their bodies forming a river. The reflective surfaces were turned skyward toward the police surveillance aircraft continually circling above the camp, returning the apparatus of surveillance back onto those watching from above. In other frontline actions, the mirrors reflected the militarized police back to themselves, attempting to interrupt the abstraction of conflict and reveal the human being behind the uniform.

The Mirror Shield Project emerged from a much larger movement of Indigenous liberation already underway at Standing Rock. The resistance to the Dakota Access Pipeline was not simply an environmental campaign, but an assertion of Indigenous sovereignty, relationship, and responsibility to land, water, and future generations. The Mirror Shield Project became Luger’s contribution to that larger movement: an artwork conceived not simply to represent resistance, but to become useful within it. A humble act of making in one place could become an act of solidarity somewhere else.

In the decade since Standing Rock, the project has continued to move between frontline action, Indigenous land and water defense, community making, performance, exhibition, and scholarship. Because the design was released as open source by the artist, its history belongs not to a single author, but to the many hands and communities that have carried it forward. Mirrored shields have appeared in Stop Line 3 actions opposing the Enbridge Line 3 pipeline, in Black Lives Matter actions across the United States, and anonymously in resistance movements around the world. In many of its museum presentations, the project has remained active rather than archival, inviting communities to make and activate new shields locally and allowing the work to move beyond exhibition spaces and back into community and social action.

At the Corcoran, Reflect celebrates this ten-year lineage while carrying the engagement ethos of the Mirror Shield Project forward. The exhibition functions as both a living archive and a working toolshed. Visitors, artists, students, and community groups are invited not only to encounter the history of the project, but to participate in its continued life through social collaboration, shield-making, and performance activation.

Ten years after Standing Rock, the full reach of the Mirror Shield Project remains impossible to trace — and that is precisely its legacy. The larger movement for Indigenous liberation continues to take new forms: asserting sovereignty, defending land and water, strengthening relationships, and imagining futures beyond colonial systems. Within the larger living Indigenous liberation movement, the Mirror Shield Project continues in motion, carried forward not through ownership, but through participation.
